book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook opens with the formulas (M1 = currency with public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI, and so on) and adds narrow/broad labels as a footnote. Here the whole is built first: the stock of money is drawn as eight boxes, the boxes get their shares, and the learner is asked where most money sits (banks' time deposits). Only then comes the problem (why not use the raw stock?) through an allowance analogy, then each aggregate is ticked off on the same eight boxes, and the narrow/broad labels are explained by the time-deposit fact learned earlier. It works because each formula is a selection from parts the learner already knows; it is weaker where the analogy is never mapped back to liquidity.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Build the whole as a fixed set of parts first, then teach each aggregate as a selection of those parts, and name each family only after its parts are visible.

moves.concept: how M0-M4 are calculated

moves.concept: how M0-M4 are calculated
moves.what: M2 = M1 + all post-office demand deposits; M3 = M1 + all banks' time deposits; M4 = M3 + post-office demand and time deposits, each said as 'M1 ke upar'.

narration.density: About 22 terms (reserve money, M0, money multiplier, high powered / basic / primary money, monetary base, monetary aggregates, stock of money, currency in circulation, deposits with RBI, bankers' deposits, other deposits, demand deposit, time / fixed deposit, postal deposits, liquidity, money supply, narrow money, broad money, NSC, M1-M4) in about 8 minutes, about 2.7 per minute, at a brisk 180+ words a minute. Heavy for a first look; the 80 s analogy is the only slow stretch, and the last two minutes pack four definitions and a caveat.

talmel_summary: Most changes land within a second of the naming word, and in the build-up parts (the eight-box tree, the shares, the rank badges, the tick table) the picture does more than write the word: it splits a box, puts a number under its part, or copies a row and adds a tick. In the analogy the picture runs 1.5-2 s ahead of the words, and the spoken 'strike out' is never shown. The 'why split by liquidity' and narrow/broad parts mostly write the narrator's sentence into boxes. Two transcript gaps (14.8-28.3 s and 285.8-300.7 s) hide the speech at the agenda and at the switch from the analogy back to money.

voice.notes: Judged from the transcript only: about 184 words a minute, brisk and conversational Hinglish with English terms (components, deposits, liquidity). Enumerates in order ('pehla component hai... doosra... chautha'), uses 'dhyan dijiye' for caveats, a rhetorical 'agar poochha jaaye' before the ranking, and 'maan lijiye' to open the story. Percentages are read plainly with 'lagbhag' for the approximate ones; formulas are said as 'M1 ke upar ... add karna hoga'. Pauses could not be judged; the second-person allowance story (aap, aapke pitaji) is the warmest stretch.

game_ideas.player_does: Builds each aggregate on the tick table: drags component tiles (public cash, banks' cash, bankers' deposits, other deposits with RBI, bank DD, bank TD, postal DD, postal TD, plus a decoy NSC tile) into the rows M0-M4; for M2-M4 the player first presses 'copy row' from the base aggregate, then adds tiles.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each row's money bar grows by the share of the parts added (bank TD makes a big jump), and the row snaps to its family (reserve, narrow, broad) with the liquidity meter beside it.
game_ideas.win: All five rows match, with M3 built on M1 (not M2) and NSC left out of M4.
game_ideas.lose: Putting bank TD into M1 turns the 'narrow money' label red and the liquidity meter drops ('this money is locked for a term'); building M3 on M2 shows an extra postal-DD tick flashing as 'not in M3'; NSC in M4 is rejected with the caveat.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a household or shop for a week of bills: each bill must be paid today, this week or this year, and the player chooses which pocket to pay from (cash in hand, bank savings/DD, bank FD, post-office deposit).
game_ideas.process_happens: Cash and DD pay at once; an FD or post-office term deposit must be broken first, with a delay and a small penalty shown, while each pocket's label shows which aggregate it belongs to.
game_ideas.win: Pay every bill on time with least penalty by using narrow-money pockets for urgent bills and leaving term deposits for later.
game_ideas.lose: Paying an urgent bill from an FD makes it late and costs a penalty, with the message that this is why time deposits sit in broad money (less liquid), not narrow money.
game_ideas.concept: reserve, narrow and broad money; M3 as money supply

game_ideas.player_does: With an allowance cut from 10,000 to 3,000 rupees, sorts expense cards into yearly, monthly, weekly and daily piles, then strikes out cards to fit the budget.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each pile shows its monthly cost; striking a card lowers the total; a final screen maps the four piles onto the four money families by how fast they can be used.
game_ideas.win: Fit within 3,000 without cutting daily essentials.
game_ideas.lose: Cutting straight from the unsorted bill removes a daily need (food) while a yearly subscription stays, and the total still overshoots: the reason to sort first.
game_ideas.concept: why split the stock: different liquidity (allowance analogy)

checks_learned: A spoken action on an on-screen object ('strike out these expenses') must have a matching motion within about 2 s; flag action verbs with no motion.
An analogy must be mapped back on screen: each analogy element (expense frequency band) needs a matching element in the concept picture (liquidity band) before the concept is named.
A caption's polarity must match the narration: run a negation check between an on-screen note and the spoken sentence it sits under (here 'not counted' vs a note that seems to say 'considered').
Shares shown as current data need a date and source tag; a number shown but only described in words ('negligible' for 5%) must be spoken or dropped.
When an aggregate is defined as 'base + part', animate the base row being copied and the new part added (worked here); a check can compare the script's 'X = Y + Z' lines with the scene's row ticks.
The stated reason for a classification should use the defining property (liquidity for narrow vs broad), not a size fact; flag 'because' clauses whose cause is not the classifying property.
Side panels of paragraph text (over about 20 words per box) should be cut to a short label plus a picture of the property.

teaching_best.why: The whole stock of money is built as eight named boxes before any aggregate is mentioned, so each formula later is just a choice of known parts.
A question to the viewer ('where is most money?') with a 1-2-3 ranking plants the fact (banks' TD is the biggest) that later explains narrow vs broad money.
A relatable second-person story (allowance cut from 10,000 to 3,000) makes the need to sort a mixed whole felt before the term 'aggregate' arrives.
Every formula is said as 'on top of M1/M3, add ...', and the table copies that row and adds one tick, so the words and the picture build the same structure.

teaching_weak.why: The analogy is never tied back: frequency of expenses is not mapped to liquidity, and the bridge falls inside a 15 s transcript gap; the 'cut to 3,000' has no counterpart in monetary policy.
Narrow money is said to exclude time deposits 'because most money is there', a size reason; the usual reason is lower liquidity. Describe, do not copy.
Shares are approximate, undated and unsourced, and the post office is given the same 85/15 split as banks.
Gold and shares are said to be outside money supply with no reason, and the on-screen note seems to say the opposite.
NSC exclusion from M4 is a bare caveat with no reason or picture; M3 not including postal DD (unlike M2) is shown in the table but never said.
